After not biking for a few years, I'm getting back into biking again as a good way to exercise and spend time with my fiancee (also blame Pokemon Go). I used to bike 20+ miles each day to get to my volunteer job when I was a teenager, but nowadays I live much closer to town and would like to bike the short 2-mile ride to work during the summer instead of driving.

One other nice addition is that my town has extended the paved bike path to cover my route, where it was partly gravel before. For this reason I'm making the switch from mountain bike to road bike, and would like to know what I should know about riding a road bike. Thank you for your time, and happy cycling!
I've recently gotten back into cycling again and ordered my first road bike. Are there any tips or tricks I should know coming from a mountain bike?
I was going to say watch out for cars but it looks like you have a separate bike path to use for your commute and Pokemon hunting.

Yessir :) nothing but me, a dedicated bike path, and a beautiful Alaskan summer. I do appreciate the safety tip though! There are some sections where I will be crossing roads - not all of them paved - for very brief periods. Does a small amount of dirt road cause any trouble for 700cc road bike tires? If so, I'll plan on taking long ways around to stay on the pavement.

My other concern is any bits of glass or sharp rocks on the path, but I'll do my best to avoid those. I haven't had any problems with the mountain bike, but that's got sturdier tires.

I envy you even more now. My father did sometimes have problems with dirt/sand on bike paths when he rode a road bike. He fell once when he turned quickly to avoid some debris and fell (sprained his hand). He was probably going to fast at the time though.

There's always room for one more in Alaska :) That's a good tip; I'll have to watch my speed and make sure I anticipate any hazards before I approach them. My main motivation for getting a road bike is that I'm usually on pavement nowadays and I've read that road bikes are a bit easier on hills.
Keep the tire pressure as high as it will go without popping the tire or pump. The stiffer tire is less likely to be cut or punctured.

I hadn't thought of that; thanks for the tip! :) I almost thought of going with a hybrid bike with sturdier tires, but I saw a road bike that appealed to me and thought "what the hell?" Besides that, I've always wanted to try the drop handlebars.

This might have been the best advice in the thread; I wanted to circle back and thank you again. I was a little uneasy about road bike tires on an mixed environment, but a well-inflated road bike tire seems to be just fine for the occasional gravel road.

I've had my bike for a few weeks and I still appreciate this advice. Most of my commute is on a dedicated bike path, but there are a few sections I have to cross the road and the well wishes are always apprciated.

not always the case, but depending on the bikes and how you're using them, the road bike in general (since you are using it every day) is going to need a bit more upkeep. i have used this for a while, http://www.londoncyclist.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2010/01/Bicycle-maintenance-made-ridiculously-easy.pdf, and it is a pretty fantastic guide to bike maintenance as a whole and, if i remember right, gives you a basic idea of how many miles/days you should go between checking the various parts.
This looks like one of those rare resources that is both comprehensive and simple. I really appreciate it!
I still have this saved on my desktop to reference when I need it. I've only had my bike for a few weeks but I know proper maintenance will extend its life and my enjoyment of it.
Don't try to ramp off of curbs with road tires. It's a lot easier for the inner tubes to explode.
Thank you, I'll keep that in mind. My route is pretty uneventful, so I should be alright :)
I think of this advice every time I ride now, no matter how tempting a worn down curb looks.

I've been away from here for a bit so I know my reply is late. I should have clarified that by road tires I meant the skinnier and flatter tires. There is less contact area, so more force on each square inch of surface.

I was used to the fat off-road tires, and tried to take a minor curb jump with new road tires and my back inner tube exploded. I only weighed maybe 120 pounds, so it shocked me. I'd assume I probably over-inflated my tires, making the blowout more likely.

No worries, and I do have some pretty skinny tires on my bike (although it's retired for the season until Alaska warms up again :P) so it's good advice. My dad bikes a lot and he recommended keeping my tires well-inflated to avoid punctures, so I keep that in mind as I'm riding as well. For flat ground, my road bike has been much better than my old mountain bike, but I know it's also less robust and I need to be a bit more gentle on it and not take road conditions for granted.

Yeah, over any significant distance road tires make the trip easier. I prefer them to mountain tires even knowing they may blow out easier without vigilance. I've not had much trouble since my first blowout, which I'd attribute mostly to my own inexperience with road tires at the time. Patching holes can be a bit trickier with less surface area for the adhesive to grip, but is still very doable if you take care to seal it properly.
